questions.prompt: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal must return a list per level, such as `[[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]`. With a `deque`, how do you know where one level ends?

choices.text: Pop nodes until the queue is empty; everything popped belongs to one level
Before each level, record `len(queue)` and pop exactly that many nodes
Start a new level whenever a popped node has no children
Store the nodes in a stack and start a new level each time it empties

questions.explanation: When a level starts, the queue holds exactly that level's nodes, because their children are appended behind them. Taking `size = len(queue)` and popping `size` nodes processes the level and leaves the next level queued. Popping until empty would mix all levels into one list. A leaf can appear in the middle of a level, so it doesn't mark the end.

questions.prompt: Why use `collections.deque` rather than a `list` as the BFS queue in Python?

choices.text: `deque.popleft()` is O(1), while `list.pop(0)` is O(n)
`deque` keeps its items in sorted order
A `list` can't hold tree node objects
`deque` uses less memory per item than a `list`

questions.explanation: BFS removes from the front and appends at the back. The Python docs say a `deque` supports O(1) appends and pops at either end, while a list incurs O(n) memory movement for `pop(0)`, because every remaining item shifts left. On a tree with many nodes, `list.pop(0)` turns an O(n) traversal into O(n²).

questions.prompt: A validator checks only that each node's children are on the right side of it (`left.val < node.val < right.val`, skipping missing children). Run it on this tree: root `5`, left `4`, right `6`, and `6` has children `3` (left) and `7` (right). What happens?

choices.text: It says invalid, which is correct, because `3 < 6` is out of order
It crashes, because `4` has no children to compare
It says valid, and it's right: every parent-child pair is in order
It says valid, wrongly: `3` sits in `5`'s right subtree but is less than 5

questions.explanation: Every parent-child pair passes: 4 < 5 < 6, and 3 < 6 < 7. But the BST property covers whole subtrees: everything in the right subtree of `5` must be greater than 5, and `3` isn't. The fix is to pass bounds down the recursion, so the node `3` is checked against the range (5, 6).

sources.claim: A valid BST has only keys strictly less than the node in its left subtree and strictly greater in its right subtree, both subtrees also BSTs, with values from -2^31 to 2^31 - 1.

questions.prompt: Explain how to check correctly whether a binary tree is a valid binary search tree, and why checking each node against its children isn't enough.

model_answer.summary: The BST property applies to whole subtrees, not just children, so pass an allowed `(low, high)` range down the recursion and check every node against it. Or do an in-order traversal and check the values are strictly increasing.
key_points: Every value in a node's left subtree must be strictly less than the node, and every value in its right subtree strictly greater
Comparing only with the direct children misses deeper violations, such as a small value deep in a right subtree
Recurse with bounds: the left child gets `(low, node.val)`, the right child gets `(node.val, high)`, starting from `(-inf, inf)`
Alternative: an in-order traversal of a valid BST is strictly increasing, so compare each value with the previous one
Both take O(n) time and O(h) stack

questions.explanation: LeetCode's definition uses strict inequalities, so a duplicate value makes the tree invalid. Using `float('-inf')` and `float('inf')` as the starting bounds avoids trouble with values at the integer limits.

questions.prompt: Which traversal solves Kth Smallest Element in a BST most directly?

choices.text: Level order, returning the k-th node dequeued
Pre-order, returning the k-th node visited
In-order, stopping at the k-th node visited
Post-order, returning the k-th node visited

questions.explanation: In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. In a BST that means values come out in ascending order, so the k-th value visited is the k-th smallest, and an iterative in-order can stop there without visiting the rest. The other orders don't follow value order.

questions.prompt: The BST `[5, 3, 6, 2, 4, null, null, 1]` has root `5`; `3` and `6` are its children, `2` and `4` are the children of `3`, and `1` is the left child of `2`. What is the 3rd smallest value?
questions.explanation: An in-order traversal visits `1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6`, and the third value is `3`. Picking `4` or `5` usually comes from counting in the order the nodes appear in the array, which is level order, not value order.

questions.prompt: In the BST `[6, 2, 8, 0, 4, 7, 9, null, null, 3, 5]` (so `4` has children `3` and `5`), what is the lowest common ancestor of `3` and `5`?
questions.explanation: Start at the root: 3 and 5 are both less than 6, so go left to 2. Both are greater than 2, so go right to 4. At 4 they split, 3 to the left and 5 to the right, so 4 is the lowest node that has both as descendants. `6` and `2` are common ancestors, but not the lowest.

questions.prompt: Walking down a BST to find the LCA of `p` and `q`, when do you stop and return the current node?

choices.text: When `p` and `q` are not both smaller and not both larger than it
When the current node is a leaf
Only when the current node's value equals `p.val`
When `p` and `q` are both smaller than the current node

questions.explanation: If both values are smaller, the LCA is in the left subtree; if both are larger, it is in the right. Otherwise they split here, or one of them is this node, and the current node is the LCA. The problem lets a node be a descendant of itself, which is why LCA(2, 4) is 2. Both being smaller is the signal to go left, not to stop.

questions.prompt: Explain the algorithm for Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree, its time and space cost, and why it doesn't work on an ordinary binary tree.

model_answer.summary: Walk down from the root, going left while both values are smaller and right while both are larger; the first node where they split (or that equals one of them) is the LCA. It takes O(h) time and O(1) space iteratively, but depends on the BST ordering.
key_points: If both `p` and `q` are less than the node, go left; if both are greater, go right
Otherwise the current node is the LCA (they split here, or the node is `p` or `q`)
It follows one root-to-node path: O(h) time, and O(1) space as a loop
It relies on the BST property to know which side each value is on
In an ordinary binary tree you must search both subtrees, which is O(n)

questions.explanation: The BST ordering lets you decide at each node where both targets must be without looking. That's the same reason search in a balanced BST is O(log n).

questions.prompt: Compare how much memory BFS and DFS need on (a) a wide, shallow tree such as a complete binary tree, and (b) a deep, narrow tree such as a long chain. Which would you pick for each?

model_answer.summary: BFS's queue holds up to a whole level, so its memory is O(width); DFS's stack holds one root-to-node path, so its memory is O(height). On a wide tree DFS uses far less; on a deep chain BFS does.
key_points: BFS memory is O(w), the maximum number of nodes on one level, because the queue holds a level at a time
DFS memory is O(h), the height, because the stack holds the current path from the root
Complete tree: the last level has about n/2 nodes, so BFS needs O(n) while DFS needs O(log n); prefer DFS
Chain of n nodes: width is 1, so BFS needs O(1) while DFS needs O(n); prefer BFS or an iterative DFS
In Python, a recursive DFS on a deep tree also hits the default recursion limit of 1000

questions.explanation: This is the exercise for the lesson. Both traversals take O(n) time; the difference is only which shape of tree makes their working set large.

questions.prompt: A perfect binary tree has 20 levels (2^20 − 1, about 1 million, nodes). Roughly how many nodes does each traversal hold at its peak: the BFS queue, and the recursive DFS call stack?

choices.text: BFS about 524,000; DFS about 20
BFS about 20; DFS about 524,000
Both about 20
Both about 1,000,000

questions.explanation: The last level of a perfect tree holds 2^19 = 524,288 nodes, and BFS has them all in its queue at once. DFS only holds the current path from the root, which is at most 20 nodes deep. So on a wide, shallow tree DFS uses far less memory, and on a deep, narrow tree the reverse is true.

questions.prompt: Which rules validate the strict BST property? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Comparing each node only with its direct children always proves the full property.
Equal keys in the left subtree satisfy the strict less-than requirement.
Ignore bounds from grandparents after descending one level.
Every left-subtree key is less than its ancestor node key.
Passing ancestor bounds catches violations beyond direct children.

questions.explanation: a is incorrect: A deeper descendant can violate an ancestor bound. b is incorrect: The given BST definition excludes equality. c is incorrect: All ancestor ordering constraints remain relevant. d is correct: The constraint covers the entire subtree. e is correct: Descendants must obey all inherited bounds.

questions.prompt: Which facts justify the BST lowest-common-ancestor search? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The LCA can never be either of the two target nodes.
When both targets are larger, the LCA search must move left.
When both target keys are smaller, search the left subtree.
A split or current target node identifies the LCA.
The same value comparison identifies target subtrees in any ordinary binary tree.

questions.explanation: a is incorrect: A target can be an ancestor of the other. b is incorrect: It must move right. c is correct: Both targets lie to that side by BST ordering. d is correct: A node counts as its own descendant. e is incorrect: An unordered tree gives no such guarantee.

choices.text: Recursive DFS has constant call-stack depth on a long chain.
A level-order queue can grow with the maximum level width.
Recursive DFS uses a call stack along the current root-to-node path.
A complete tree necessarily gives recursive DFS linear stack depth.
